subject: ss-plastic-surgery
title: Principles of Flap Physiology and Classifications

steps.tx: The **reconstructive ladder** establishes the classical hierarchical framework in reconstructive surgery, progressing methodically from primary wound closure and healing by secondary intention to skin grafts, local flaps, regional flaps, and microvascular free tissue transfer. Modern reconstructive surgery frequently adopts the reconstructive elevator, selecting the optimal functional reconstruction immediately.
steps.say: Every wound is climbed the same way. The reconstructive ladder starts with simply sewing it shut, then letting it granulate, then skin grafts, local flaps, regional flaps, and finally free tissue transfer at the top. Modern surgeons ride the elevator instead, jumping straight to whichever rung fits the defect best.

nodes.label: Primary closure or healing by secondary intention
Skin graft: split or full thickness

steps.tx: Cutaneous **random pattern flaps** derive their entire arterial inflow and venous drainage through the interconnected dermal and subdermal vascular plexus without a distinct named feeding vessel. Due to perfusion pressure drop across the microcirculation, cutaneous random flaps are traditionally designed with length dimensions rarely exceeding a two-to-one ratio relative to width on trunk tissues.
steps.say: A random pattern flap has no named artery and lives entirely off the fine mesh of vessels under the skin. Because pressure fades as blood crosses that mesh, keep the flap short and broad, rarely more than twice as long as it is wide on the trunk, or the tip will die.

vis.alt: Split thickness skin grafting and dermal vascular plexus bed
vis.caption: Cutaneous vascular plexus and dermal perfusion in skin resurfacing. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: In contrast, an **axial pattern flap** receives robust vascular supply from an anatomically defined arteriovenous vessel running along the longitudinal flap axis. This dedicated axial vessel ensures high perfusion pressure and reliable venous return, permitting surgeons to harvest significantly longer flap dimensions without conforming to arbitrary length-to-width restrictions.
steps.say: An axial flap brings its own named artery running down its length, so pressure stays high all the way to the tip. With a dedicated vessel aboard, the surgeon can draw a far longer flap and ignore the two-to-one rule that governs random flaps.

steps.tx: The **Mathes and Nahai classification** categorises muscle and musculocutaneous flaps into five distinct vascular patterns. **Type I** muscle flaps receive blood supply from an isolated solitary vascular pedicle, as observed in the tensor fasciae latae nourished by the lateral circumflex femoral artery and the gastrocnemius muscle nourished by the sural system.
steps.say: Mathes and Nahai sorted every muscle flap by its blood supply into five types. Type one is supplied by a single pedicle alone, like the tensor fasciae latae on its lateral circumflex branch or the gastrocnemius on its sural vessels.

steps.tx: Muscle flaps with **Type II** vascular anatomy feature a dominant pedicle sustaining muscle viability and minor secondary pedicles that are divided during elevation, such as the gracilis, trapezius, and soleus muscles. **Type III** muscle flaps possess two dominant pedicles of equal caliber, exemplified by the gluteus maximus and rectus abdominis.
steps.say: Type two muscles have one dominant pedicle plus minor ones that can be sacrificed, such as gracilis and soleus. Type three muscles carry two equal dominant pedicles, the rectus abdominis and gluteus maximus being the great examples, so either end can survive alone.

vis.alt: Surgical soft tissue harvest and vascularised flap transfer
vis.caption: Reconstructive tissue transfer and recipient bed preparation. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.tx: Under the Mathes and Nahai system, **Type IV** flaps possess segmental pedicles along the muscle length without any dominant pedicle, exemplified by the sartorius and tibialis anterior. Division of more than two segmental branches compromises perfusion. **Type V** flaps have one dominant pedicle and secondary segmental pedicles, notably the latissimus dorsi.
steps.say: Type four muscles have no dominant vessel at all, just a row of equal segmental branches feeding the sartorius or tibialis anterior, and cutting more than two of them kills the muscle. Type five, led by the latissimus dorsi, enjoys one dominant pedicle backed by segmental helpers.

steps.tx: The physiological **surgical delay phenomenon** enhances flap survival by converting borderline ischaemia into enhanced collateralisation. Performing partial incisional incisions or staged elevation 10 to 14 days prior to definitive transfer induces ischaemic stress that permanently dilates choke vessels between adjacent angiosomes, increasing the reliable flap survival length.
steps.say: A flap that barely reaches can be trained to survive further. Cut its borders but leave it in place for ten to fourteen days, and the ischaemic stress permanently widens the choke vessels into the next territory, stretching the safe length, which is the surgical delay.

nodes.label: Transient ischaemic stress and choke vessel dilation
Definitive flap transfer at 10 to 14 days

steps.tx: Postoperative flap monitoring assesses microvascular perfusion using clinical evaluation of skin color, surface capillary refill, tissue turgor, and needle prick bleeding. **Venous thrombosis** presents acutely with cyanotic dusky congestion, rapid capillary refill under 1 second, tissue swelling, and brisk dark-purple venous bleeding on pinprick, mandating immediate surgical re-exploration.
steps.say: After inset, the flap must be watched like a hawk. A vein that clots turns the flap dusky purple and swollen, with lightning-fast refill and dark brisk bleeding on pinprick, which is venous congestion demanding an immediate return to theatre before the flap is lost.
